**Audience**: an engineer who already runs a ViT or a ResNet and wants to read — and reproduce — the pivotal papers. **Empirical first**: each topic starts from a result that does not hold up, such as a fine-tuning gain from ImageNet to a business domain that turns into a loss when the batch size changes, or a contrastive pre-training that "cheats" through a leak in the augmentations; only then do we name the tools that explain it: experimental protocol, ablations, the architectures and objectives themselves.

The module is a reading seminar on ViT, ConvNeXt, self-supervision, mixtures of experts and large-scale training.

### What you will be able to do

-   Place the pivotal papers (ViT, DeiT, Swin, ConvNeXt, MoE, SimCLR, MAE, DINOv2, MobileNet) in their lineage and their legacies.
-   Compare architecture families on measurable criteria rather than on an isolated benchmark.
-   Explain the two major families of self-supervision — contrastive and masked — and their trade-offs in data and compute.
-   Dissect an experimental protocol and distinguish the demonstrated contribution from the packaging.
-   Use training recipes at scale and interpret scaling laws.
-   Replicate an experiment from a paper and report on it reproducibly.
-   Explain the founding objects of the official research themes — symmetry and equivariance, robustness, neural fields, analysis-by-synthesis, amortized inference, sampling, physics-informed learning.
-   Present a research paper in writing and orally, in the seminar's format.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026-2027 catalog)

According to the [CSC_52087_EP — “Apprentissage profond avancé”](https://synapses.polytechnique.fr/catalogue/2026-2027/ue/16172/CSC-52087-EP-apprentissage-profond-avance) sheet: the official objective is to initiate students into the advanced principles of deep learning — mathematical foundations, architecture design and practical applications.

The description stresses that the field moves at a very fast pace, with new techniques and architectures appearing constantly, and that future practitioners must keep up with the latest advances; the assessment combines homework, quizzes and team projects; the language is English.

The keywords are deep learning, transformers, computer vision and symmetry in deep learning. The detailed programme lists nine themes, with the initials of the instructor in charge; the table maps each of them, in the sheet's order, to the section that teaches it.

The sheet names the themes only, so the content of each section is our reading of its title; the 2026–2027 instructors may treat a theme from another angle. *Complement to the official programme —* the seminar chapters on the experimental protocol (ch. 1), the replication project (ch. 2), ConvNeXt (ch. 5), mixture of experts (ch. 6) and training at scale (ch. 9) do not appear in the published themes; they are the method and the background that the reading of the themed papers relies on.

### Where this course fits in the program

An option of period 2 of M1, outside the recommended track. Official prerequisites: not communicated (the “Prerequisites” tab of the SynapseS sheet is empty); in practice, the official description addresses students already initiated into deep learning. The foundation — backpropagation, CNNs, attention, training in practice — comes from the P1 [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html) module, whose necessary elements (transformers, optimization, normalization) are reactivated in chapter 0. It is the Deep Learning course of every student of this option: Deep Learning P2 belongs to the same P2 choose-1 group, so choosing this course in P2 implies Deep Learning in P1.

Downstream, this module directly prepares [Advanced Topics in Large Language Models](../m2-advanced-topics-llms/index.html) (M2), which extends the critical reading of papers on the LLM side, and above all the research track of the master's program: the seminar format and the replication project are its methodical training.

Chapter 10 (neural fields, analysis-by-synthesis, sampling, physics) touches the subjects of Image Synthesis and Multimodal Generative AI. Both are options of the same choose-1 group, so a student takes only one of the three: this page is self-contained with respect to them, and their chapters are optional reading (section 10.6). The generative themes continue in the M2 module [Control in Generative AI](../m2-control-generative-ai/index.html).

### Course outline

-   **Refresher: transformers, optimization, normalization** — the P1 foundation brought back to the level of rigor that reading papers requires.
-   **Reproducible research: experimental protocol** — seeds, datasets, honest measurements: the rules of experimental proof.
-   **Projects: read, explain, replicate** — the final project: choose a paper, explain it, replicate one of its experiments.
-   **Efficient architectures: MobileNet and distillation** — cutting costs for embedded targets and transferring knowledge from a large network to a small one.
-   **Vision Transformers: ViT, DeiT, Swin** — the transition from convolutions to attention in vision, generation after generation, then the symmetries built into representations and robustness to perturbations.
-   **Modern convnets: the ConvNeXt lesson** — what transformers taught convnets, and the modern rereading of CNNs.
-   **Mixture of Experts (MoE)** — growing capacity by conditioning the computation per expert, without exploding the cost.
-   **Self-supervision I: contrastive (SimCLR and its lineage)** — learning representations by bringing views of the same image closer together.
-   **Self-supervision II: masking (MAE, BEiT, DINOv2)** — learning by reconstructing the invisible, up to the DINOv2 lineage.
-   **Training at scale: recipes and scaling laws** — the practical rules of heavy training and the laws linking size, data and performance.
-   **Beyond recognition: neural fields, inference, sampling and physics** — coordinate networks, analysis-by-synthesis through differentiable models, amortized inference, sampling as a design choice, physics-informed learning, and where to pursue the generative themes in the other modules.
-   **Course research notes (Kalogeiton, Lutzeyer, Zhu)** — the papers of the module's instructors (and of Xi Wang), read with the same grid.
-   **Exercises** — short applications to anchor each paper.
-   **References** — the papers and sources of each chapter.

### Session plan {#sessions}

**38.25 h in class = 9 sessions of 4.25 h.** The volume is the one of the SynapseS 2026–2027 sheet (38.25 h: 18 h of lectures and 20.25 h of exercise sessions), which we read as nine weeks of a 2 h lecture followed by a 2.25 h exercise session.

The sheet's detailed programme lists nine themes without dates; the plan follows their order — symmetry (session 3), robustness (4), self-supervision (5–6), neural fields and analysis-by-synthesis (7), amortized inference, sampling and physics (8) — with one exception: distillation, the seventh theme, is taught in session 2 with efficient architectures, because its accounting is used by chapters 4 to 6 and teaching it after the generative themes would make the difficulty go back down.

The seminar's own chapters (protocol, ConvNeXt, mixture of experts, scale) are interleaved where they are needed, and the split into sessions is our proposal. Since the course is a reading seminar, the research notes of the instructors (ch. 11) are taught in class.

Level 1 = foundations (refresher, protocol, accounting), 2 = the pivotal papers, 3 = research themes and critique; the level never goes down from one session to the next.
